title: What is the difference between {{ }} and {!! !!} in laravel blade files?

content:
# Escaping Versus Raw Output in Laravel Blade When building views with Laravel, you will inevitably encounter two distinct syntaxes for injecting data into HTML: `{{ }}` and `{!! !!}`. While they may look similar at a glance, the distinction between them is fundamental to preventing security vulnerabilities and controlling how your server processes content. Understanding when to use which is not just a stylistic choice; it is a critical requirement for secure application development. The core difference lies in how Laravel handles HTML escaping. When you wrap a variable in double curly braces `{{ }}`, Laravel automatically escapes the output using PHP's `htmlspecialchars` function. This process converts special characters like ampersands (`&`) and angle brackets (`<`) into their corresponding HTML entities (e.g., `&`, `<`). The primary goal here is security. By default, this prevents Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks by ensuring that any user-generated content cannot be interpreted as executable JavaScript or HTML tags by the browser. If you are outputting data from a database or form input, `{{ }}` should almost always be your default choice. Consider a scenario where you are displaying a blog post title fetched from a database: ```blade

{{ $post->title }}

``` If the database contains the string ``, this syntax will render it as plain text: `<script>alert('XSS')</script>`. The browser displays the characters literally rather than executing the script. This safety net is built into the framework, saving you from manually calling `e()` (the legacy escape helper) or worrying about encoding issues. Conversely, `{!! !!}` disables this automatic escaping. It tells Laravel to output the variable exactly as it exists in memory, treating the content as trusted raw HTML. This syntax was introduced to handle cases where you genuinely need to render complex HTML structures generated by external libraries or specific formatting requirements that `htmlspecialchars` would break. For example, if you are rendering a rich text editor's output or a third-party widget that requires unescaped tags: ```blade
{!! $editorContent !!}
